en: Yeah, no, it's a great question. Huntress is an amazing company. I was fortunate to spend a little bit of time working at ForgePoint, which invested in Huntress. Especially if you are running in a customer's environment, you have to balance like, do I detect all the things or do I detect what I'm good at? Because if I detect all the things, I promise you, because no two enterprise environments are the same. You're going to lead to a bunch of false positives. So every vendor has to run this very fine Pareto front of finding the optimal space. Which again, if I'm starting to cut stuff at some point, I'm going to miss things. So the real example here is, we'll focus on something topical like OpenClaw. So when OpenClaw first deployed, came out, right? Really exciting, cool productivity piece, nightmare for security teams. What we were able to do that no other system could was, we'd actually built some really comprehensive machine learning models around command line investigation and in GenSec systems, as it just so would happen, run command lines. We could actually see when the OpenClaw agent wasn't doing things like it should, like catching an OpenClaw agent touching a production DB. The second piece really is focusing on what we call the telemetry, right? The raw data itself. So most security vendors, right? Back to that Pareto front, generate detections, they'll generate alerts but because they can't catch everything, there's this whole swath of data that is undiscovered, right? That doesn't really remain touched and our whole process is to constantly look at that data and go, what might be amiss, and use data inputs like context from the customer organization, right? They can upload a threat model or intelligence, right? What are bad actors doing with existing tools that are running on this system? And then finally, we've got a brilliant group of folks that do research and test, and build these agents. So we have these three new axes that surface things that otherwise might have gone missed and to that end, you know, over our company's lifecycle. We've run over three hundred million agentic investigations, and we've surfaced over four thousand active incidents that had otherwise gone missing.

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Oh, man. All right, cool. Well, I think at least I get it now. That's the good thing. That's, you know, one person gets it now. But so that's, I guess, the core idea. Maybe walk me through even just how you make the decision. This is what, 2024 at this point? Like mid-24?
zh: 哦，天哪。好，酷。好，我想至少我现在懂了。这是好的一面。你知道，现在有一个人懂了。所以我想，这就是核心想法。也许带我走一遍甚至只是你怎么做决定。这是什么时候，2024 年这个时候？比如 24 年中？

speaker: Damien Lewke
en: Yeah.
zh: 是的。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: How do you make the decision, which is always the key moment of, do you just kind of cold turkey it? Okay, I'm going all in, screw it, or you kind of phase it in. How do you play that out going from employee to founder?
zh: 你怎么做决定，这总是关键时刻，你是直接当机立断吗？好，我要 all in，去他的，还是你逐步过渡。你怎么走完从员工到创始人这一步的？

speaker: Damien Lewke
en: Yeah, great question. So ultimately I can only speak from my experience, but I definitely ascribe to the cold turkey school of thought. So, you know, my decision point basically is I got really quiet with myself and asked myself, if I made $0 and all I could do was tackle this problem. Would I do it, right? If I could accept that I would get no monetary benefit, but I could focus on this problem full time. Would I do it? And the answer was yes, that's when I made the jump. The best advice I can give to a prospective founder is be obsessed with the problem and not inherently your solution. Because your solution will evolve and change over time. If you're calling all the shots a couple of years in, you might want to ask yourself why that's the case. But for me, it was the obsession with the problem and just going, you know what, I got to do this. And thankfully, I made the jump and I'm very grateful that I did. It is a moment of uncertainty. It can be a bit scary when you got forty bucks in your bank account. You're like, oh, gosh, I hope this works. But it has been by far the most rewarding experience.
zh: 是的，好问题。所以最终我只能从我的经验出发说，但我绝对信奉当机立断这一派。所以，你知道，我的决定点基本上是我让自己非常安静下来，问自己，如果我赚到 0 美元，而我所能做的就是攻克这个问题。我会做吗，对吧？如果我能接受我不会得到任何金钱回报，但我可以全职专注于这个问题。我会做吗？答案是会，那就是我跳下去的时候。我能给未来创始人最好的建议是，痴迷于问题本身，而不是天然地痴迷于你的解决方案。因为你的解决方案会随时间演变和改变。如果你入行几年后还是你在拍板所有决定，你可能得问问自己为什么会那样。但对我来说，那是对问题的痴迷，然后就是，你知道吗，我必须做这个。谢天谢地，我跳了，我非常感激我跳了。那是一个充满不确定性的时刻。当你银行账户里只有四十美元的时候，会有点吓人。你会想，哦，天哪，我希望这能成。但迄今为止这是最有回报的经历。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: But I would argue for somebody in your position who's doing something in their industry. Worst case scenario, a year later, it doesn't work. You're probably extremely hireable. You've got that kind of the downside protection. Which is different than if you go, and this is the good thing about going into your industry. When you decide like, oh, screw it, I'm gonna start a marketplace for whatever, right? And then you try to come back. It's a little tougher.
zh: 但我会说，对于处在你这个位置、在你自己行业里做事的人来说。最坏的情况，一年后没成。你大概率还是极其容易被雇用的。你有那种下行保护。这不同于如果你去做——这是进入自己行业的好处之一。当你决定，哦，去他的，我要为一个什么东西开个平台市场，对吧？然后你再想回来。就有点更难了。

speaker: Damien Lewke
en: It certainly is. I will say this for what it's worth as a hiring manager. I actually am always excited to meet founder curious people or former founders. We have a former founder on staff here. You are also extremely hireable if you try something and it doesn't necessarily work out. Because the problem solving and skill sets that you build and learn, honestly, you know, there's that expression, right? We learn far more from failure than we do from success. To me, that says a lot about your character. So it's definitely something that I totally get but yes, you're right.
zh: 确实是。就我的观点而言，作为一名招聘经理我想说，我其实总是很乐意见到有创始人意向的人或前创始人。我们这里就有一位前创始人在职。如果你尝试了某件事而它没有真正成，你也依然极其容易被雇用。因为你所构建和学到的问题解决能力和技能组合，说实话，你知道，有那句话，对吧？我们从失败中学到的远多于从成功中学到的。对我来说，这说明了很多关于你品格的东西。所以这绝对是我完全理解的事情，但是的，你是对的。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: I mean, I tend to agree. It always depends on the employer. You know, the bigger company or a small, but for a startup. I can tell you for our companies, the first ten, twenty hires, if they could be all founders, I'd probably be for it, right? We just try, and it's just because the level of management a founder needs, frankly, is zero and so somebody gone out for a year or two years, and done something on their own. It's like, okay, I know I can be like, this is the thing you're doing, and they're just going to go run off and do, which is amazing.
zh: 我是说，我倾向于同意。这总是取决于雇主。你知道，大公司还是小公司，但对于初创公司。我可以告诉你，对于我们的公司，最初的十名、二十名员工，如果他们可以全是创始人，我大概会赞成，对吧？我们就是试试，而这只是因为创始人所需要的被管理程度，坦率地说，是零。所以有人出去了一年或两年，自己做了些事情。那就是，好，我知道我可以，这是你在做的事，然后他们就会自己跑去做，这太棒了。

speaker: Damien Lewke
en: Yeah, a hundred percent, right? And early days, you have to have that kind of flexibility, right? You're wearing a million different hats. There's no structure. Having somebody who can just take something and run with it is invaluable to a startup.
zh: 是的，百分之百，对吧？而在早期，你必须有那种灵活性，对吧？你戴着几百万顶不同的帽子。没有结构。有一个能拿走一件事就直接跑起来的人，对一家初创公司来说是无价的。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: So, we're going through the story. So you've decided that you're going to leave. Are you alone? Do you have a co founder at the outset? What's the setup?
zh: 那么，我们继续过这个故事。所以你已经决定要离开。你是一个人吗？你在起步时有联合创始人吗？是怎样的配置？

speaker: Damien Lewke
en: First time solo founder. So it was just me.
zh: 第一次做 solo founder。所以只有我。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Oh buddy, going on hard mode, I like that.
zh: 哦兄弟，开启困难模式，我喜欢。

speaker: Damien Lewke
en: Yeah, I have conviction, I had conviction and you know, at the time it was the right choice. And I backed that up.
zh: 是的，我有信念，我当时有信念，你知道，在那时那是正确的选择。我用行动证明了它。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: And you're technical, so you could build the stuff and try to sell it? You could do both those things?
zh: 而且你是技术型的，所以你能构建这些东西并尝试卖出去？你能同时做这两件事？

speaker: Damien Lewke
en: Yes, so again, fortunate in that regard where being technical I have the ability to kind of sit across both. But one of the core functions as we built this company is I've continuously hired myself out of a job, right? Hired myself out of the marketing leader role and we've got an amazing head of engineering, product, sales, customer success. That's been my constant focus, right? It's ultimately to bring people who are more skilled and more accomplished in each of these roles to develop that. But yeah, in the beginning, I sat across everything. Which was interesting.
zh: 是的，所以再说一次，在这方面很幸运，作为技术型我有能力横跨两头。但在我们构建这家公司的过程中，一个核心职能是我持续地把自己从岗位上雇出来，对吧？把自己从市场负责人的角色里雇了出来，我们有一位了不起的工程负责人、产品、销售、客户成功负责人。这是我持续的焦点，对吧？归根结底就是把在每个角色上更熟练、更有成就的人带进来来发展它。但是的，一开始，我横跨所有事情。那挺有意思的。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: I mean, I love that and I actually want to take a tangent on this. Because it's more and more popular that, I mean, solo founders have always been a thing but I think with AI, there's just a rise. Statistically, there's just more and more solo founders. And especially, I would assume that a lot of that increase is actually from the non technical who before, could not start a startup without a technical co founder. Now they're like, wait a second, I could actually build a product. I could deploy something on my own. The question I have is, how have you, specifically, because there's different, you know, people play things different. I'm curious on how you did it. The fact is you therefore start with more equity, which is great. But you have more gaps, more holes to fill. If you're three co founders in theory, I'm like, I'm the salesperson, I'm the product person, I'm the CEO. Whatever it is, right? And so you're like, okay, cool, we don't need to hire VP sales, we don't need to hire VP. Did you therefore hire heads of earlier? Did you give them bigger equity grants than they would have gone into another startup that has two or three co founders? How did that end up playing out for you?
zh: 我是说，我很喜欢这一点，我其实想在这个话题上跑个题。因为这越来越流行了，我是说，solo founder 一直存在，但我觉得随着 AI，出现了一波增长。从统计上看，solo founder 就是越来越多。尤其我会猜，其中很多增长其实来自非技术型的人，他们以前没有技术联合创始人就无法创办初创公司。现在他们想，等一下，我其实可以构建一个产品。我可以自己部署一些东西。我的问题是，你 specifically，因为不同的人有不同的玩法。我很好奇你是怎么做的。事实是你因此起始时拥有更多股权，这很棒。但你有更多缺口、更多洞要填。如果你有三个联合创始人，理论上，我是说，我是销售、我是产品的人、我是 CEO。不管是什么，对吧？所以你会想，好，酷，我们不需要招 VP 销售，我们不需要招 VP。那你因此更早招了负责人吗？你给他们的股权比他们加入另一家有两三个联合创始人的初创公司更大吗？这一切最后对你来说是怎么演变的？

speaker: Damien Lewke
en: Yeah, you know, I've always focused on needs based hiring. I think that's another thing too is when you're especially early, you need to be pretty litigious about capital management. But yeah, I mean, my focus was to give folks who are coming in. Because it's earlier and it's riskier, compelling offers, right? To me, I've always believed, and my team knows this. Compensate the folks well. I think one well placed person is far better than four poorly placed people and that's why I think one of the most overlooked but valuable skill sets for a founder is to run an extremely diligent and focused recruitment process. Because you want to be certain. Because when you're six people, that seventh person is, you know, fifteen percent of your business. You want to make sure that you're doing the right thing.
zh: 是的，你知道，我一直聚焦于按需招聘。我觉得这也是另一件事，尤其是在早期，你需要对资本管理非常谨慎。但是的，我是说，我的重点是给进来的人。因为更早、风险更高，有吸引力的条件，对吧？对我来说，我一直相信，我的团队也知道这一点。把人酬劳给好。我觉得一个放对位置的人远好于四个放错位置的人，这就是为什么我觉得创始人最被低估但最有价值的技能组合之一，是运行一个极其勤勉和专注的招聘流程。因为你要确定。因为当你只有六个人的时候，第七个人就是，你知道，你业务的百分之十五。你要确保你在做对的事。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: I guess, I ask it from the perspective, like, I'll give you the anecdote and curious if you have something similar to this. Maybe in a different role, like, founder I work with closely. Solo founder, non-technical, hired, you know, there were maybe fifteen people, twenty people, and they hired a VP. And some of the people I reached out to, to say, hey, do you have a good VP, blah, blah, blah. They're like, dude, it's so early. Why are you hiring a VP when you have fifteen people? And I'm like, the answer is you're looking at it from your perspective of me and my co founder, right? We split the roles and effectively they were operating as a VP. And so we didn't have a VP until we were fifty. Yeah, okay but this person is a solo founder. Therefore they hired these heads up earlier. I'm curious if you had anything like that. Maybe not on the VP side, but whether on the sales or marketing, or not really. If you think like compared to somebody who had two or three co-founders, it was actually, you build the org in a similar way, sort of thing.
zh: 我想，我是从这个角度问的，比如，我给你一个轶事，好奇你有没有类似的。也许在不同的角色上，比如，一位和我紧密合作的创始人。Solo founder，非技术，雇了，你知道，大概十五个人、二十个人，然后雇了一位 VP。而我联系的一些人，去问，嘿，你有没有好的 VP， blah blah blah。他们说，兄弟，这么早。你只有十五个人为什么要招 VP？然后我想，答案是你站在你和你的联合创始人的角度看这件事，对吧？我们分了角色，实际上他们在扮演 VP 的角色。所以我们直到五十人的时候才有 VP。是的，好吧但这个人是 solo founder。因此他们更早招了这些负责人。我很好奇你有没有类似的情况。也许不在 VP 层面，而是在销售或市场层面，或者并没有。如果你想想，和一个有两三个联合创始人的人相比，实际上是，你以类似的方式搭建组织，诸如此类。

speaker: Damien Lewke
en: You know, I'd say we definitely did it a little bit earlier, right? As a solo founder, the way that I've always thought about it is, I visualize it as either like a balloon or a bucket but it's basically how and where am I spending my time. And how, and where should I be spending my time, right? Where is there becoming an increasing need for the business such that we need to bring in somebody full time. So, you know, our Head of Eng. was first. We were nine people at the time. I was an engineering manager, I was our salesperson, we were still in stealth. It's not much marketing, but I was doing all the things and we just got to a point. We were all engineers at the time, where I was like, it's time to bring in an effective engineering leader but also, this is a personal belief. Bring in somebody who can grow with this business, right? That's why I actually like your VP of Eng. anecdote of, it doesn't matter about size of team. It's, hey, bring in the right person and ideally bring in somebody who can grow with this business. Because as I tell everybody here at Nebula, my desire is to build an environment and a business such that they are here for a good time, and a long time. And can grow as we grow. So that was really the thought process and the management of the team had gotten to the point. Where I was like, I can be of more service to this business if we bring in the right personnel and bring in somebody who's going to run this team, and scale it. And our head of engineering has done exactly that.
zh: 你知道，我想说我们确实做得稍微早一点，对吧？作为 solo founder，我一直思考它的方式是，我把它可视化为像一个气球或一个桶，但它基本上是我在如何以及在哪里花费我的时间。以及我应该如何、在哪里花费我的时间，对吧？业务在哪里出现了日益增长的需求，以至于我们需要引入一个全职的人。所以，你知道，我们的工程负责人是第一个。我们当时有九个人。我是工程经理，我是我们的销售，我们还在 stealth。没多少市场营销，但我在做所有的事情，然后我们到了一个节点。我们当时全是工程师，我就在想，是时候引入一位真正有效的工程负责人了，而且，这是我个人的信念，引入一个能与这门业务一起成长的人，对吧？这就是为什么我其实很喜欢你那个 VP of Eng. 的轶事，重点不在于团队规模。而是，嘿，引入对的人，理想情况下引入一个能与这门业务一起成长的人。因为正如我对 Nebula 这里的每个人说的，我的愿望是构建一个环境和一门业务，让他们在这里既能过得开心，又能待得长久。并且能随着我们的成长而成长。所以那真的是思考过程，而对团队的管理已经到了那个节点。我意识到，如果我们引入合适的人员，引入一个会运营这个团队并把它规模化的人，我能为这门业务提供更多价值。而我们的工程负责人恰恰做到了这一点。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Yeah, I fully agree. One of my number one things for these heads of roles is their network. For Head of Eng., it's yeah, okay, you know, this, that management, whatever. But can you bring in the next five engineers without running a full outbound process? Because that is going to dramatically increase your, not just odds of success, but just your rate, right? If like, I need two more engineers and this person is like, well, let me ping ten people that I already know and work with. That's going to be a huge difference maker. So I always find that that's a big one. Last question then on this kind of hiring tangent. How do you think about where to hire? Do you hire where, let's say you're really good at the thing you're really good at that. You've solved and now you can bring somebody in and you go to the next fire, or do you hire for the fires? In other words, I'm incredible at sales, so I'm going to figure out a sales machine and then once sales is figured out. I'm going to come and bring somebody in who can take over. I'm going to move to the next unsolved problem versus I'm going to stay in sales because I'm great at sales and I'm going to hire somebody else. Which of the two philosophies do you typically go for?
zh: 是的，我完全同意。对于这些负责人角色，我的头号考量之一就是他们的网络。对工程负责人来说，是，好，你知道，这个那个管理能力什么的。但你能不跑一个完整的 outbound 流程就引入接下来五名工程师吗？因为那会极大地提升你的，不仅是成功的几率，还有你的速度，对吧？如果是我需要再要两名工程师，而这个人是，嗯，让我 ping 一下我已经认识并共事过的十个人。那将是巨大的差别因素。所以我一直觉得那是一个大项。那这个问题 tangent 的最后一个问题。你怎么考虑在哪里招人？你是在哪里招——比如你真的很擅长那件你真正擅长的事。你已经解决了，现在你可以引入某个人，然后你去下一个火场，还是你为火场招人？换句话说，我在销售上极强，所以我要搞出一台销售机器，然后一旦销售搞定了。我就来引入一个能接管的人。我会转向下一个未解决的问题，而不是我要留在销售因为我很擅长销售然后我去雇别人。这两种哲学你通常选哪一种？

speaker: Damien Lewke
en: Yeah, I mean, as a founder, I think one of the most important parts of your job is trying to see around the corner, right? So you said hire for the fires. I like hiring for the fires. I think the way that we thought about it, again, using the VP or the Head of Eng., discussion, right? Was I could see around the corner and go like, okay, more of my time now that we've got a big enough team is going to be spent more on sales and marketing. And at some point we're going to launch this company. I need somebody who can take and run with engineering. And I think it's important to do that because as a founder, you have a responsibility to create an environment where when you bring in anybody. An IC or a leader, you give them the agency to be successful. So I think the key is you want to bring them in at a time that the business is still growing and there's room for growth versus like, oh my God, everything is broken. Please fix this brokenness. Because then you get caught up in tactics and really what you want to do is bring somebody in and allow them to grow with that position. So hire for the fires.
zh: 是的，我是说，作为创始人，我觉得你工作中最重要的部分之一就是努力看到拐角之外，对吧？所以你说了 hire for the fires。我喜欢为火场招人。我觉得我们思考它的方式，再说一次，用那个 VP 或工程负责人的讨论来说，对吧？是我能看到拐角之外，然后想，好，现在我们有了足够大的团队，我更多的时间将花在销售和市场。而且在某个时点我们要发布这家公司。我需要一个能接过工程并跑起来的人。我觉得这样做很重要，因为作为创始人，你有责任创造一个环境，让你引入的任何人。一名 IC 或一位领导者，你给他们成功的主观能动性。所以我觉得关键是你要在他们进来的时机上，让业务还在增长、还有成长空间，而不是，哦天哪，一切都坏了。请修复这些破烂。因为那样你会陷进战术里，而你真正想做的是引入一个人并让他们随着那个职位一起成长。所以，为火场招人。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: But you'd rather be the one that figures out the unsolved part and bring somebody in to run with the thing that's already working versus the opposite?
zh: 但你更愿意做那个把未解决的部分搞清楚的人，然后引入某个人来接管已经在运转的东西，而不是反过来？

speaker: Damien Lewke
en: Yeah, a hundred percent, right? Your fundamental job as a founder is two things. Number one, create an environment where people feel seen, heard, and empowered to do their best work. And number two, to de-risk the business. You are always selling and my focus is on the unknowns, to de-risk this business to ensure that we can continue executing.
zh: 是的，百分之百，对吧？作为创始人，你的根本工作是两件事。第一，创造一个让人们感到被看见、被倾听、并被赋能去做出最佳工作的环境。第二，给业务降低风险。你永远都在销售，而我的焦点放在未知数上，降低这门业务的风险，以确保我们能继续执行。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: So back to the main storyline, you're the solo founder and you got the thesis. You've jumped fully on board on this. What's step one?
zh: 那回到主线故事，你是 solo founder，你有了论点。你完全跳上了这条船。第一步是什么？

speaker: Damien Lewke
en: Yeah, step one, customer discovery. If there is one takeaway for anybody who's listening, if you haven't read it, read a book called The Mom Test. It is, in my opinion, the best book on customer discovery that is out there. Followed by The Challenger Sale, but that's a sales book. Yeah, I kicked off what I called the ninety in ninety. Ninety customer interviews in ninety days. So I spent ninety days mom testing people. So not going to them saying, hey, my name is Damien, I've got this idea, this is what it is, can you please tell me you like it? But rather going, hey, I'm thinking about this space. Talk to me about how you've solved this problem. How would you rank this in order of priorities? Where would I focus on if we were to build something like this? And most importantly, friends, if you're doing customer discovery, always ask at the end if they're willing to introduce you to somebody else in network. Because not only does that build a relationship with this person, but it means that you also get routed to other like minded folks. zh: 千分之千是这个答案,Pablo,对吧?随着你建立关系,人们更愿意帮忙,而我最终做的,尤其是如果那次通话特别好。我们和九十场九十场中的大约十五家公司做了更深入的探讨,我和它们有两、三、四次会面。我们做一个小时,深入到一些更具体的策略。就是这样我们找到了第一批设计合作伙伴。给创始人的一个建议。走出这把椅子、走到外面去,这对我很有帮助。我骑自行车、打 Uber、坐火车、坐飞机去见这些人,这真的、真的很有帮助。因为,尤其是在今天这个分布式世界里,那些面对面的连接,听着,你需要真诚,对吧?但是,如果你真心走出去,付出时间和努力,人们会积极地回应这一点。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Was this for the first meetings or you did it only for the second meetings? How did you make this happen?
zh: 这是针对第一次会面,还是你只对第二次会面这么做?你是怎么做到的?

speaker: Damien Lewke
en: It varies. So one of the key things that I benefited from was there was a core industry conference about two months into the ninety and ninety called Black Hat that happened for us, and I just, on my own dime. Flew out to Black Hat, got myself a hotel room, paid for my Ubers and I just walked the floor. I walked up to strangers and I was like, hey, I'm Damien. Can I get you a coffee? But it was putting myself in those positions to be successful. So it was for plenty of first meetings and yes, definitely for second meetings. We had a bunch of folks, I'm based in Boston, Massachusetts. We had a bunch of folks in Boston and it was like, hey, this was great. Hey, do you want to go for a run? You want to grab a coffee? And then I'd get out there and meet them where they were in their respective city.
zh: 不一定。让我受益的关键事情之一是,在九十场九十场进行到大约两个月时,有一个叫 Black Hat 的核心行业会议,我自己掏腰包。飞去 Black Hat,自己订了酒店房间,自己付 Uber 费,然后我就在会场里走。我走向陌生人,说,嘿,我是 Damien。我能请你喝杯咖啡吗?但这就是把自己放在能成功的位置上。所以很多第一次会面是这样,是的,第二次会面肯定也是。我们有一群人,我住在马萨诸塞州波士顿。我们有一群人在波士顿,就会说,嘿,这次聊得真好。嘿,你想去跑步吗?想喝杯咖啡吗?然后我就会跑到他们各自所在的城市去见他们。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: After these ninety days, first of all, is it just you? Do you raise money? Do you have customers? What's the outcome?
zh: 在这九十天之后,首先,只有你一个人吗?你融资了吗?有客户了吗?结果是什么?

speaker: Damien Lewke
en: Yeah, so I ended up raising money during the ninety and ninety.
zh: 是的,我最终在九十场九十场期间融到了钱。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: How much did you raise?
zh: 你融了多少?

speaker: Damien Lewke
en: Yeah, so we raised a pre-seed to start. This is a $2.4 million pre seed led by Decibel, which is an AI and cyber VC. They're our day one investor. Back to obsession with a problem. I guess ours was a slightly different experience. I did not write a pitch deck. I wrote a manifesto is what I call it, but a thirty page document on why this company needs to exist, why the market is broken and starting to get early customer feedback into that. I'm kind of right place, right time. An investor came along and was like, oh, this is great. Let's do this.
zh: 是的,我们先融了一轮 pre-seed。这是一轮 240 万美元的 pre-seed,由 Decibel 领投,它是一家 AI 和网络安全的风险投资基金。他们是我们第一天的投资人。回到对问题的着迷。我们的经历稍微有点不同。我没有写 pitch deck。我写了一份宣言,我是这么叫它的,一份三十页的文档,讲为什么这家公司需要存在,为什么市场是坏的,并开始把早期客户反馈融入其中。我算是占了天时地利。一位投资人找上门来,说,哦,这很棒。我们做吧。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: You published this or they just came inbound and you sent it to them?
zh: 你发布了这个,还是他们主动找上门来,然后你发给他们的?

speaker: Damien Lewke
en: They came inbound.
zh: 他们主动找上门的。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Okay.
zh: 好的。

speaker: Damien Lewke
en: And we talked it out, yeah. They kind of found me right place, right time and, you know, what ended up happening, of course, as we raised the pre-seed. I brought in my first three hires and, you know, then we started cooking, right? The ninety and ninety had finished. We had a general idea.
zh: 然后我们聊了出来,是的。他们算是找到了我,天时地利,你知道,最终发生的事情,当然是,我们融了 pre-seed。我招进了前三名员工,然后我们开始干活了,对吧?九十场九十场已经完成。我们有了一个大致的想法。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: And timeline wise, by the way. This pre-seed is what? End of '24?
zh: 顺便问一下时间线。这个 pre-seed 是什么时候?24 年底?

speaker: Damien Lewke
en: No, like July, August '24.
zh: 不,大概是 24 年 7、8 月。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Okay, mid 24. Okay, got it.
zh: 好的,24 年年中。好的,明白了。

speaker: Damien Lewke
en: Mid '24, and then along the way, you know, we did the ninety and ninety, we start building and then we were fortunate to have Bain Capital Ventures come in and preempt our seed round as well.
zh: 24 年年中,然后在这一路上,你知道,我们做了九十场九十场,我们开始构建,然后我们有幸让 Bain Capital Ventures 进来,preempt 了我们的 seed 轮。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Which was when?
zh: 那是什么时候?

speaker: Damien Lewke
en: End of '24.
zh: 24 年底。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: And that was another what? Like, $4 million?
zh: 那又是多少?比如,400 万美元?

en: $6.1 million. So we were $8.5 million raised, yeah, so.
zh: 610 万美元。所以我们总共融了 850 万美元,是的,所以。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Where were you at customer wise in that second half of '24?
zh: 在 24 年下半年,你的客户情况如何?

speaker: Damien Lewke
en: So we signed our first design partner when we had one employee, which was cool. It was actually at Black Hat. I can't share their name, but they are a paying customer now, and I'm very grateful for their early partnership. And actually it was really helpful, right? Before you even can deploy, cause the product was so early. You know, I pitched it as an architecture partnership. Hey, do you just want to give feedback while we start poking around and building this? It was so valuable. We had a few key early architecture partners back then and it made such a difference, Pablo. Because, yeah, we've done the ninety-ninety, we had the roadmap, but to keep getting feedback continuously, right? Just allowed us to, not just in terms of how the system worked, but customer experience, build right from the outset, which was really, really awesome to see.
zh: 我们签下第一个设计合作伙伴时只有一名员工,这很酷。其实是在 Black Hat 上。我不能透露他们的名字,但他们现在是付费客户了,我非常感激他们的早期合作。这真的很有帮助,对吧?在你甚至还没法部署之前,因为产品非常早期。你知道,我把它包装成一种架构合作伙伴关系。嘿,你愿不愿意在我们开始摸索和构建的时候给我们反馈?这太有价值了。我们当时有几个关键的早期架构合作伙伴,这带来了巨大的不同,Pablo。因为,是的,我们做了九十九十,我们有路线图,但要持续不断地获得反馈,对吧?让我们不仅在系统如何运作方面,还在客户体验方面,从一开始就构建正确,看到这个真的非常棒。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Tell me more about these. Everyone is doing design. I mean, you used to do beta, you know, and now you do design partnerships, architecture, whatever. Everyone's doing them and one of the challenges I have as VC looking at these is which ones are meaningful signal and which ones are just kind of playing along. It's not a high bar, generally speaking. It depends on the type of customer, obviously, but it's not the highest of bars to get somebody to be like, yeah, I'll use your product and give you feedback. I'm curious, your experience, how did you know that the feedback was real, that the pull was real, that the value was truly there and that many of these would convert to paying customers?
zh: 跟我多讲讲这些。所有人都在做设计。我是说,你以前做 beta,你知道的,现在你做设计合作伙伴、架构,随便什么。所有人都在做,而我作为 VC 看这些的一个挑战是,哪些是有意义的信号,哪些只是随便陪跑。一般来说门槛不高。当然取决于客户类型,但让某个人说,好的,我会用你的产品并给你反馈,这不是最高的门槛。我很好奇你的经历,你怎么知道反馈是真的,拉力是真的,价值确实存在,而且这些很多会转化为付费客户?

speaker: Damien Lewke
en: I mean, I'm actually excited to say that every single one of our design partners converted to a paying customer and that was a really, really exciting moment. But I work with a lot of founders now who are thinking about design partnerships. Because our design partner program did end up being effective. My suggestion is you actually have to break up design partnerships into stages. Early on your design partnership, you are not sending them a POC document that says you will be entitled to a discount after this time, right? You don't have something to sell yet. The idea is, hey, we're going to work through this and eventually you set the expectation. I'm going to send this and you will get a discount, right? Once this product goes live. But it starts with architectural partner. Early design partner. Hey, we've deployed it. Does this work? How is the deployment process? Are things breaking? How is your experience?
zh: 我是说,我其实很兴奋地说,我们的每一个设计合作伙伴都转化成了付费客户,那是一个非常、非常激动人心的时刻。但我现在和很多正在考虑设计合作伙伴的创始人合作。因为我们的设计合作伙伴项目最终确实有效。我的建议是,你实际上必须把设计合作伙伴分成阶段。在设计合作伙伴早期,你不会给他们发一份 POC 文档,说你在某个时间之后有权享受折扣,对吧?你还没有可以卖的东西。想法是,嘿,我们会一起推进这个,最终你设定预期。我会发这个,你会得到折扣,对吧?一旦这个产品上线。但它从架构合作伙伴开始。早期设计合作伙伴。嘿,我们部署了。这能用吗?部署过程如何?有东西坏了吗?你的体验如何?

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: And the ask is probably what time touch points? If somebody is not responding, you're like, okay, let's not invest our time there.
zh: 而要求大概就是投入多少时间吧?如果某人不回应,你就会说,好吧,我们不要在那儿投入时间了。

speaker: Damien Lewke
en: Yeah, you want to keep it super tight. So I get them to commit to thirty, or I got them to commit to thirty minutes every single week. I will not miss the meeting. Please don't miss the meeting. Let's do thirty minutes a week and most people are willing to find thirty minutes. And I would challenge, especially early on, if someone is not willing to give you thirty minutes a week. How much do they really value the problem you're solving? And then the final phase, which was as we were starting to shift into paying customers towards the end of last year. It was kind of end of summer into fall. It was really more feature design partners. Hey, we're building this thing, right? What's your feedback on this? What else do we need to do to earn this price that we've suggested? And that's really how we made the transition. So you want to phase the design partner approach and don't overcomplicate it, right? Ask for time, they'll commit to time. You build a relationship and eventually, if what you do is valuable, they will pay for it.
zh: 是的,你要保持非常紧凑。所以我让他们承诺三十,我让他们承诺每周三十分钟。我不会缺席会议。请你也不要缺席会议。我们每周做三十分钟,而大多数人都愿意挤出三十分钟。我会挑战一点,尤其在早期,如果某人不愿意每周给你三十分钟。他们到底有多在意你正在解决的问题?然后是最后阶段,就是在我们开始向付费客户转变的时候,大概去年年底。大概夏末到秋天。那时更多是功能设计合作伙伴。嘿,我们在构建这个东西,对吧?你对这个的反馈是什么?我们还需要做什么才能赢得我们建议的这个价格?这就是我们完成转变的方式。所以你要给设计合作伙伴的方式分阶段,不要过度复杂化,对吧?要时间,他们会承诺时间。你建立一段关系,最终,如果你做的东西有价值,他们会为它付钱。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: When did you start? When did you get your first revenue?
zh: 你什么时候开始的?你什么时候拿到第一笔收入?

speaker: Damien Lewke
en: Yeah, Fall of last year.
zh: 是的,去年秋天。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: So there was a year of, you raise your pre seed and then a few months go by, you do design partnerships probably Q4 of '24, Q1 of '25, those six months, is that right?
zh: 所以中间有一年,你融了 pre-seed,几个月过去,你在大概 24 年 Q4、25 年 Q1 做设计合作伙伴,那六个月,是这样吗?

speaker: Damien Lewke
en: Yeah, I mean, it was basically a year of design partners before we saw revenue. But the key was, it was a personal opinion, I wanted to get to a point where the revenue was a slam dunk and no brainer. Because ultimately, once you get on the revenue train in a startup, you got to start scaling.
zh: 是的,我是说,在我们看到收入之前,基本是整整一年的设计合作伙伴。但关键是,这是个人观点,我想达到一个收入是毫无悬念、不用大脑思考的地步。因为最终,一旦你在创业公司里踏上了收入的列车,你就得开始规模化。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: The clock is ticking and it's a funny thing you say. You really want to almost like you pulling it back. So when you let go, it's like whoof.
zh: 时钟在滴答,而且你说的是个有趣的事。你真的想要几乎像把它往后拉。这样当你放手的时候,就是嗖地一下。

speaker: Damien Lewke
en: It's funny because it also teased out a really important piece of product market fit for us, which was building a repeatable POC process. So the idea, because we kept iterating through these design partnerships, right? And seeing what worked, and the cadences, was it allowed us to start structuring a real proof of concept process. So net new, if we were to engage, how do we engage? And, you know, back to this original point of, hey, what was your moment of Product Market Fit? By the time we hit that Fortune 500, we had a month long POC process that required two hours of customer time. We had a playbook that we knew how to run and it just kind of followed, right? That muscle movement had been built.
zh: 有趣的是,它也为我们勾出了产品市场契合中一个非常重要的部分,那就是建立一个可重复的 POC 流程。这个想法是,因为我们在这些设计合作伙伴中不断迭代,对吧?看到什么有效,那些节奏是什么,这让我们得以开始构建一个真正的概念验证流程。所以对于全新的客户,如果我们要接洽,我们如何接洽?然后回到最初那个问题,嘿,你的产品市场契合时刻是什么?等我们拿下那个财富 500 强时,我们有了一个只需要客户投入两小时、为期一个月的 POC 流程。我们有了一套我们知道如何执行的 playbook,它就这么顺下来了,对吧?那个肌肉动作已经建立起来了。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: And that was when? That Fortune 500 customer?
zh: 那是什么时候?那个财富 500 强客户?

speaker: Damien Lewke
en: March of this year.
zh: 今年三月。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: March of '26. So a year after, let's say, you converted those first design partnerships. This moment happened. You had a year of, in production and trying out different POC structures to get there.
zh: 26 年三月。所以在那之后一年,比如说,你转化了那批最早的设计合作伙伴之后。这个时刻发生了。你有一年在生产环境里、尝试不同 POC 结构的经历才走到那一步。

speaker: Damien Lewke
en: Yes. Oh, and Pablo, did we try a bunch of different structures.
zh: 是的。哦,Pablo,我们可是试了一大堆不同的结构。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Tell me, you know, this is. By the way, another deep dive we're going to do. Because I've seen it firsthand. Again, there's bars, right? The bar to get somebody to be a beta customer design partnership is here. The bar to get a POC is there. The bar to get production level is that much higher and a lot of people get stuck somewhere in between. POCs, notoriously, you can just get them to be dragged out. Where it's like, well, somebody's not going to sign a POC if they're not interested. So clearly they're interested. So clearly it's going to convert at some point, but then maybe it doesn't. Maybe it takes six months. Maybe you don't have six or twelve months or whatever it is. So finding a way to lock that in where I've got a company right now I can think of firsthand that had to just iterate on so many different, then it got stuck at pricing. Then it got stuck on IT. Then it got stuck on whatever it is on legal and you're like, well, I don't understand why somebody would run a three month pilot. Get value, by the way, because the thing worked and it's been six months now, and they still haven't converted. So I would love to understand what you went through, the stuff that you tried that didn't work, and then what you ultimately ended up with that is now rinse and repeat.
zh: 跟我讲讲,你知道,这个是。顺便说,这是我们要做的另一次深挖。因为我亲眼见过。再说一次,门槛在那里,对吧?让某个人成为 beta 客户、设计合作伙伴的门槛在这里。拿到 POC 的门槛在那里。拿到生产级别的门槛又要高得多,而很多人卡在中间某处。POC 是出了名的容易被拖得很长。就是那种,嗯,如果对方没兴趣,是不会签 POC 的。所以显然他们有兴趣。所以显然它会在某个时候转化,但然后也许没有。也许要花六个月。也许你没有六个月或十二个月或不管多久。所以要找到一种方式锁定它,我现在 firsthand 就能想到一家公司,不得不迭代了那么多不同的东西,然后卡在定价上。然后卡在 IT 上。然后卡在法律上,不管是什么,你就想,嗯,我不明白为什么有人会跑一个三个月的试点。拿到价值,顺便说一句,因为那个东西是好使的,而现在已经六个月了,他们还是没转化。所以我很想了解你经历了什么,你尝试过哪些没用,然后你最终得到了现在可以重复使用的那套东西。

speaker: Damien Lewke
en: I do just want to say I'm very grateful for our paying customers. But to be quite honest, Pablo, there were a few POCs that went three or six months or dragged out. And they dragged out really because of three core reasons. One, we were all excited but what I didn't do is set good expectations around, hey, this is how long the POC process is going to be. This is what we are doing and at this point, this will be done. The second piece, and it's just the way that we work, was also being really focused about scope of engagement. That does not mean you should pressure somebody in a POC to purchase your solution. I do not espouse the idea of like, it's two weeks, you agree to these success criteria, buy my thing. That's not cool, especially early, right? But you do want to set expectations. Hey, we're going to do this for a month. If we do things one, two, three, right? Would you move to a purchase? Which leads me to my third and the most important thing from the outset that goes back to this Fortune 500. Which is make sure that you have budget, or that they have the ability to spend money on what it is that you have built. Because there are a lot of people who are really helpful and extremely friendly, and they're down to do a POC. Sometimes they don't have budget or budget won't free up until later in the year. No harm, no foul. If you set a scope for the POC, great, you can get the tech win and move on with your life. And then you know that when the budget comes up, we have this agreed to, we can press go. The other piece that I think really helped us, and because we're an AI-native company, is really important. Is, nail your DPA, right? Have a really strong DPA, and know what it means to do data processing, and parallelize the legal paperwork. Do not do the POC and then suddenly be like, all right, hey, oh, by the way, we do data processing. They go, well, hey, wait a minute, we have our own DPA. This happened with one of our customers who I love, but we did a POC and we got to this point where it was like, great, we signed some stuff. Oh, now we have to go into procurement and some businesses will operate that way, right? And you cannot help that. That's okay. But as best as you can, it doesn't hurt at all to just ask like, hey, while we do this process, can I either do the procurement paperwork up front. So that the POC can roll over and do a paid engagement? Or can we run these two things alongside? That will not always be the case, but it will save you time and heartache. Because the worst anyone can say is no and that's okay. You're in the spot you were in before.
zh: 我确实想说一句,我非常感激我们的付费客户。但老实说,Pablo,有几个 POC 拖了三个月或六个月。它们拖长主要是因为三个核心原因。第一,我们都很兴奋,但我没有做的是设定好的预期,比如,嘿,这个 POC 流程会有多长。这是我们在做的,到了这个节点,这个会完成。第二部分,这也和我们的工作方式有关,是对接洽范围保持非常聚焦。这不意味着你应该在 POC 中给某人施压去购买你的解决方案。我不认同那种,只有两周,你同意这些成功标准,买我的东西。那不厚道,尤其在早期,对吧?但你确实要设定预期。嘿,我们要做这个一个月。如果我们做到一、二、三,对吧?你会转向购买吗?这就引出我的第三点,也是从一开始就最重要的一点,又回到那个财富 500 强。也就是确保你有预算,或者他们有能力在你构建的东西上花钱。因为有很多非常乐于助人、极其友好的人,他们很乐意做 POC。有时他们没有预算,或者预算要到今年晚些时候才能腾出来。没有伤害,没有过错。如果你为 POC 设定了范围,很好,你可以拿到技术上的胜利,然后继续自己的生活。然后你知道,当预算出来时,我们已经就这个达成一致,我们就可以按下开始。另一件我认为真正帮到我们的,而且因为我们是一家 AI 原生公司,这一点真的很重要。是,搞定你的 DPA,对吧?拥有一份非常强有力的 DPA,知道做数据处理意味着什么,并且把法律文书并行化。不要做完 POC 然后突然说,好了,嘿,哦,顺便说一句,我们做数据处理。对方说,嗯,嘿,等一下,我们有我们自己的 DPA。这件事发生在我们的一个客户身上,我很喜欢他们,但我们做了 POC,然后到了这个地步:很好,我们签了一些东西。哦,现在我们得进入采购流程,有些企业就是这么运作的,对吧?你帮不了这个。没关系。但尽你所能,问问完全不吃亏,比如,嘿,在我们做这个流程的同时,我能不能把采购文书提前做掉。这样 POC 就能滚动进入一个付费接洽?或者我们能不能把这两件事并行推进?这不总会成功,但它会为你省下时间和心痛。因为对方最坏的反应就是说不,而那也没关系。你还在你之前的位置上。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: So that's the high level and I think all that obviously foots. Take one of the examples you mentioned. Some of these did take three, six, nine months. There's no point in naming names. It's not the point. But take one of those examples. Let's go deep on it. What happened? Why did it take so long? And maybe what could you have done differently? And I'm sure you now do those things differently, but you just kind of get specific on one of them.
zh: 这是高层的情况,我认为这一切显然都说得通。拿你提到的一个例子。有些确实花了三、六、九个月。没必要点名。那不是重点。但拿其中一个例子。我们深入聊聊。发生了什么?为什么花了这么久?也许你本可以做什么不一样的?我相信你现在做这些事情的方式不同了,但你就具体讲讲其中一个。

speaker: Damien Lewke
en: First of all, I love this customer and they are great. The real learning for me was I did not determine and figure out what the path to close is or was from a procurement point of view. So we spend so much time mapping stakeholders within the org and who has budget authority and all that stuff. And don't think at all about procurement, and legal process, and system. So basically we did the POC, it was a design partnership that became a POC, and they were like, yup, we love this, we want to buy. Great, let's buy. Cool, can you send us your MSA? We're going to send this to procurement.
zh: 首先,我很喜欢这个客户,他们很棒。对我来说真正的教训是,我没有从采购的角度确定并弄清楚成交的路径是什么。所以我们花了很多时间在组织内部梳理利益相关者,谁有预算权限和所有那些东西。却完全没有考虑采购、法律流程和体系。所以基本上我们做了 POC,那是一个变成 POC 的设计合作伙伴,他们说,是的,我们喜欢这个,我们想买。很好,我们买吧。很酷,你能把你们的 MSA 发给我们吗?我们要把它发给采购。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: And you've done the work of saying, hey, this is the champion. This is who has budget, CIO has budget, blah, blah. So you knew that part of it.
zh: 而你已经做了功课,说,嘿,这是支持者。这是有预算的人,CIO 有预算,等等。所以你了解了那部分。

speaker: Damien Lewke
en: Budget agreed to, champion agreed to.
zh: 预算同意了,支持者同意了。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Got you.
zh: 明白了。

speaker: Damien Lewke
en: All right, let's send it in for procurement. Hi, procurement, here you go and that was it, right? There was no like, hey, who should I be working with? Hey, should I, our champion was awesome. But there was also an executive sponsor that we should have worked with, right? Is there anyone I can do? So basically, what ended up happening, Pablo, was there was like this black hole of procurement. There was my champion, who is an amazing human being. Who can't push procurement, and we just had to work through their machinery, and it took weeks to get something turned around. Once we got it, we needed to make a bunch of edits and we ended up going through a few different iterations or red lines. And it just ended up dragging out. And it's because while I figured out my champion internally, what I didn't do was identify if there was another executive sponsor I could loop in and I didn't ask about their procurement process. I didn't know who the stakeholders were. I didn't know who I should be working with, you know, and who I should be introduced to. I just kind of was like, here you go. I hope this closes. There's no urgency. That was the problem and the key learning for me was, always have an executive sponsor and ask him about the procurement process. It's okay, I have been a customer before of security solutions. I was not always thrilled with my procurement process and that's not to say the procurement teams are bad. I love procurement teams. They're amazing people. But they have a responsibility to do what's right for the business and if you're an early stage company, they're going to push back. So it's important to understand who you're working with on the procurement side. That was the key learning.
zh: 好的,我们把它发给采购吧。你好,采购,给你,然后就这样了,对吧?没有那种,嘿,我应该和谁合作?嘿,我要不要——我们的支持者很棒。但其实还有一个我们应该合作的执行发起人,对吧?有什么我能做的吗?所以基本上,最终发生的事情,Pablo,是采购像一个大黑洞。有我的支持者,他是个很棒的人。但他推不动采购,我们不得不跟他们的机器硬磨,一个东西 turnaround 要花好几周。等我们拿到它,我们需要做一堆修改,最终经历了好几轮迭代或红线修改。然后就一直拖着。这是因为虽然我在内部搞清了我的支持者,但我没做的是确认是否有另一个我可以拉进来的执行发起人,而且我没问他们的采购流程。我不知道利益相关者是谁。我不知道我应该和谁合作,你知道的,以及我应该被介绍给谁。我基本上就是,给你。我希望这能成交。没有紧迫感。那就是问题所在,对我来说关键的教训是,永远要有一个执行发起人,并问他采购流程。没关系,我以前也当过安全解决方案的客户。我对我的采购流程也不总是感到兴奋,这不是说采购团队不好。我喜欢采购团队。他们是很棒的人。但他们有责任为企业做正确的事,而如果你是一家早期公司,他们会推回来。所以理解你在采购那边和谁合作很重要。那就是关键的教训。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: I love that example. I think especially founders who have never worked at large companies forget just how large companies work and the fact is, first of all, obviously not everybody knows everybody. Second of all, not even everybody is a friend. They're not all swimming in the same direction where it's like, oh, if John really likes it, I'm in procurement. You know, I love John. I'm going to help John make this happen because that's my job. It's like, my thing is this thing. I'm interested on this thing over here. So you as the founder have to basically figure out, okay, the champion is the thing I think that we've all collectively learned. We know you need a champion in order to close an account. Cool, great, I've heard this thing from somebody that does enterprise. Who's the anti champion? Who's going to be the person, whereas the thing moves ahead, they're going to be like, nope, we're not doing this because whatever and how can you pre block that, right? So procurement is one obvious one. Legal is another one. IT, these are three buckets of people who, generally speaking, tend to be, let's say, or are potentially going to be on the other side. Being this person saying, wait, but it's an early stage company. It's risky, wait, but they don't have SOC 2. They don't have this, they don't have that, whatever. It's a cyber issue and go figure out how you can get that intro instead of six months down the road when you're like, okay, this is going to close next week. As early as humanly possible and go make friends. Make friends in as many possible places, right? So that the thing gets pushed through.
zh: 我喜欢这个例子。我认为尤其是那些从没在大公司工作过的创始人，会忘记大公司到底是怎么运作的，事实是，首先，显然不是每个人都认识每个人。其次，甚至不是每个人都是朋友。他们并不是都朝同一个方向使劲，不是那种“哦，如果 John 真喜欢它，我在采购部门，我爱 John，我要帮 John 把这事办成，因为那是我的工作”。而是“我管的是这个东西，我感兴趣的是那边那个东西”。所以你作为创始人基本上得搞清楚，好的，拥护者（champion）这个东西我想是我们大家都集体学到了。我们知道你需要一个拥护者才能成交一个客户。好，很好，我听做企业级销售的人说过这个。那谁是反拥护者（anti champion）？谁会是那种，当事情往前推进时，会说“不，我们不干这个，因为如此这般”的人？你怎么能提前堵住这一点，对吧？所以采购是一个显而易见的，法务是另一个，IT，这是三类人，一般来说，往往——或者说有可能——会站在对立面。当那个说“等等，可这是一家早期公司，有风险。等等，可他们没有 SOC 2，他们没有这个，没有那个，随便什么。这是个网络安全问题”的人。去搞清楚你怎么能拿到那个介绍，而不是六个月之后，你才说“好吧，这个下周就要签了”。要在人力所能及的最早时间，去交朋友。在尽可能多的地方交朋友，对吧？这样事情才能被推过去。

speaker: Damien Lewke
en: And this is why it really helps. For our first, I think our first like eight customers. I flew to meet them before we decided to send in the PO. Genuinely, it's funny, you know, I like my blank and blank. I did a five and five. I did five cities in five days. I flew to the West Coast, down the West Coast, back to the Midwest, and then back to the East Coast, right? I did like a cross country marathon to meet with customers. Because it allowed me to have these kinds of conversations and, again, build real relationships. That is another core piece. Again, early stage, people are investing in you because they trust you. It is your responsibility to be genuine and build real relationships.
zh: 这也是为什么这真的很有帮助。我们的头一批，我记得是头八个客户，在我们决定发出 PO 之前，我都飞过去见他们。真的，很有意思，你知道，我喜欢我的什么什么。我做了一个五和五。五天跑了五个城市。我飞到西海岸，沿着西海岸南下，回到中西部，然后再回到东海岸，对吧？我做了一场横跨全国的马拉松来见客户。因为这让我能进行这样的对话，并且，再说一次，建立真正的关系。这是另一个核心要素。再说一次，早期阶段，人们投资的是你，因为他们信任你。你有责任做到真诚，并建立真正的关系。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: And so now are you doing this? Going to what works? And besides just having, you know, saying, okay, the pilot is like this, it's this long, et cetera, et cetera. Do you then go out and meet? Have you identified kind of every department that could block it and you're going in, and meeting them. Whether it's in person or virtual, whatever, and just trying to figure out who the key stakeholder is going to be along the entire way from zero to, you know, signed full contract?
zh: 那现在你在做这个吗？去做有效的事？除了——你知道——除了说“好的，试点是这样的，时长是这么多”等等等等。你之后会出去见面吗？你有没有识别出每一个可能卡住它的部门，然后去，去见他们。无论是线下还是线上，随便什么方式，就是试图搞清楚从零到，你知道的，签署完整合同这一路上，关键的利益相关者会是谁？

speaker: Damien Lewke
en: Yeah, as best we can, right? You're not necessarily going to understand everything in every capacity, but if I can't meet you in person. I will take the time to catch up with you one on one. We now have an amazing sales leader and sales team that we're building, and scaling. It's a whole thought process around kind of when and how, and why I hired salespeople when I did. But yeah, I mean, I flew to meet a customer for 24 hours last week, right? Got on a late night flight, got back on a late night flight and every bit matters. And it was with the team and we got them lunch, and we spent some time with enablement. And also just spent some time asking about their lives, and how they're doing. And at the end of the day, we're all just people and I care about what we do and that we can make people's lives better. So it was important to build that relationship and I'm still getting on planes, Pablo.
zh: 是的，尽我们所能，对吧？你不一定能在每一种情况下都理解所有事情，但如果我不能当面见你，我会花时间和你一对一沟通。我们现在有一位很棒的销售负责人和一支我们正在打造、正在扩张的销售团队。关于我在什么时候、怎么以及为什么雇了销售，这里面有一整套思考过程。但是，是的，我是说，上周我为了见一个客户飞了 24 小时，对吧？搭了深夜航班去，又搭深夜航班回来，每一分努力都有意义。是和团队一起，我们请他们吃了午饭，我们和 enablement 团队花了些时间。也花了些时间聊聊他们的生活，问问他们过得怎么样。说到底，我们都是人，我在乎我们做的事情，在乎我们能让人们的生活变得更好。所以建立那种关系很重要，而我仍然在上飞机，Pablo。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: And for context, what kind of ACVs are we talking about? That you're doing all this work for?
zh: 顺便问一下，我们在说的是什么样的 ACV？让你为这一切费这么大功夫？

speaker: Damien Lewke
en: Yeah, I mean, so in the beginning, you'll take any budget. But, you know, flexing into six figures for sure. These ACVs, and this is what I'm really encouraged by, is our ACV is continuing to climb and becoming extremely significant. Which is great proof of the problem we're solving.
zh: 是的，我是说，一开始，有多少预算你都要。但是，你知道，肯定已经伸进六位数了。这些 ACV，而这也是让我真正感到鼓舞的，是我们的 ACV 在持续攀升，变得非常可观。这是我们正在解决的问题的很好证明。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: So you're coming into like $50k, $100k, but then obviously there's expansion later. That's kind of the bucket you're playing in.
zh: 所以你进来的时候是大概 5 万、10 万美元这种，但显然之后会有扩张。这就是你所处的那个区间。

speaker: Damien Lewke
en: Yeah, I mean, we've now closed and we've got several more coming. But we've closed several six figure deals now, and in the beginning, yeah, I'll take $20k, $30k if you'll give it to me. You take whatever you get. We're now at the point that we've proved the value and demonstrated something that is able to command a higher ACV. But the key is you got to build something that's valuable. You can't just be like, oh, it's this much because, right? You want to have value based metrics that show why people should pay that.
zh: 是的，我是说，我们现在已经签成了，还有好几单在路上。但我们已经签成了好几单六位数的交易，而在开始的时候，是的，只要你肯给，2 万、3 万我也拿。你拿到什么就要什么。我们现在到了已经证明了价值、展示出了能够支撑更高 ACV 的东西的阶段。但关键是，你得打造出有价值的东西。你不能就说“哦，就这个价，因为如此这般”，对吧？你要有基于价值的指标，能说明人们为什么该付那么多钱。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: You talked about revenue acceleration later and kind of waiting until you could really grow fast. How fast did you hit a million ARR?
zh: 你后来谈到了收入加速，以及要等到你才能真正快速增长。你用了多久达到 100 万 ARR？

speaker: Damien Lewke
en: Yeah. So, I mean, we're still scaling. So I can't really comment on ARR right now, but we've got a pretty aggressive target that we're looking for. The key really with scale is always to stack your pipeline and make sure as you get customer adoption that you're able to commit to that scaling process.
zh: 是的。那么，我是说，我们仍在扩张中。所以我现在没法就 ARR 发表评论，但我们有一个相当激进的目标在追求。规模化的关键始终是堆厚你的 pipeline，确保随着客户采用的增长，你能够承诺那个扩张的过程。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Perfect, well, I'll ask the last question we tend to end on. Which is what would be your top piece of advice for an early stage founder who's kind of still looking for and finding Product Market Fit?
zh: 好，那么我来问我们通常用来收尾的最后一个问题。也就是，对于一个还在寻找和探索 Product Market Fit 的早期创始人，你最重要的建议是什么？

speaker: Damien Lewke
en: Continuous customer discovery. It doesn't matter if you have a solution built. I mean, people use product market. Product Market Fit is honestly a journey. You have moments where you see that you have it and we experienced that. But we got there because of, gosh, at the time, twenty one months of constant customer discovery. I think the best thing, if you got thirty minutes or an hour and you're not sure what to do with your time. Get on the phone with a prospect, get on the phone with a customer and ask them. That is the best thing that you can do is continuous customer discovery.
zh: 持续的客户发现。你有没有把解决方案做出来不重要。我是说，人们嘴上说 Product Market——老实说，Product Market Fit 是一段旅程。你会有一些时刻看到自己拥有了它，我们经历过。但我们能走到那一步，是因为，天哪，当时是二十一个月持续不断的客户发现。我认为最好的事情是，如果你有三十分钟或一个小时，不知道该拿这些时间干什么，就给一个潜在客户打电话，给一个客户打电话，问他们。你能做的最好的事情就是持续的客户发现。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Perfect, man. Well, Damien, thanks so much for jumping on the show, dude. It's been great.
zh: 好，兄弟。那么，Damien，非常感谢你来上节目，老兄。真是太棒了。

speaker: Damien Lewke
en: Pablo, it was a pleasure. Thank you so much for having me.
zh: Pablo，很荣幸。非常感谢你邀请我。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Wow, what an episode. You're probably in awe. You're in absolute shock. You're like, that helped me so much. So guess what? Now it's your turn to help someone else. Share the episode in the WhatsApp group you have with founders. Share it on that Slack channel. Send it to your founder friends and help them out. Trust me, they will love you for it.
zh: 哇，多么精彩的一期。你可能正感到震撼。你可能彻底惊呆了。你会说，“这对我帮助太大了。”那么猜猜怎么着？现在轮到你去帮助别人了。把这期节目分享到你和创始人朋友们建的 WhatsApp 群里。分享到那个 Slack 频道。发给你那些创始人朋友，帮他们一把。相信我，他们会为此爱死你的。
